opus-5.5.text:
Part of it was very practical. A lot of developers have already built their applications around the OpenAI API, and many have learned to think about a knob that trades off quality against latency and cost. If we want people to try Mercury, the easiest thing is to make it a drop-in replacement: change the base URL, maybe the model name, and everything else keeps working. Inventing a brand-new parameter with diffusion-specific semantics would have added friction for no real benefit to the user.

The deeper reason is that the concept maps naturally onto how diffusion models work. With an autoregressive model, extra inference compute usually means generating more tokens, so you get longer chains of thought before the final answer. With a diffusion model you also have that option, but there's another axis that's native to the architecture: the number of denoising steps. We start from a noisy draft of the whole output and refine it in parallel. More refinement steps generally means higher quality, fewer steps means faster. So there's a real, continuous dial on test-time compute built into the model, and "reasoning effort" is a good abstraction to put on top of it.

From the user's point of view, they shouldn't have to care whether quality comes from more refinement passes, more reasoning tokens, or some combination. They care about the outcome: low effort for something snappy, like autocomplete or a voice agent, and high effort for a hard coding or math problem where they'll accept waiting a bit longer. Exposing it through a familiar parameter lets us optimize what happens under the hood, and change it over time as we learn better ways to spend compute, without breaking anyone's integration.

There's also a point about where diffusion shines. Because we're so fast at baseline, even our high-effort settings can land at latencies comparable to a fast autoregressive model's default. That gives developers a wider range on the quality-speed curve, and a standard knob is the clearest way to let them pick a point on it.

r001.rationale: The response says developers can keep their existing OpenAI-based applications and adopt Mercury by changing the base URL or model name, avoiding friction from a new parameter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so there were really two things going on there, a practical one and a more conceptual one.

The practical one is pretty simple. Almost everyone who's building on top of language models today is building against the OpenAI API shape. Their code already knows what a chat completion looks like, it already has a notion of a reasoning-effort knob from the o-series and the GPT-5-era models. If we had invented our own parameter, something like "number of diffusion steps" or "denoising schedule," we'd be asking every developer to learn a new abstraction and rewrite their integration just to try us out. We wanted Mercury to be a drop-in replacement. You change the base URL and the model name, and everything else keeps working, including the dial you already use to trade off cost and latency against quality.

The more interesting part, though, is that the knob actually maps very naturally onto what a diffusion model is doing under the hood. In an autoregressive model, "reasoning effort" usually means "generate more hidden chain-of-thought tokens before answering." It's effort in the form of length. In a diffusion language model, the fundamental lever is different. We start from a fully masked or noisy sequence and refine the whole thing in parallel over a number of steps. More steps means more rounds of the model looking at its own draft and correcting it. Fewer steps means you accept a rougher draft faster. That's a very clean, very direct notion of inference compute. It's not a trick layered on top, it's the core algorithm.

So when a user sets reasoning effort to low, we're running a shorter refinement schedule and you get the extremely fast decoding that people associate with Mercury, over a thousand tokens per second on H100s. When they set it to high, we're running more denoising iterations, sometimes with a different noise schedule, and the model gets more chances to catch inconsistencies, fix a variable name that doesn't match, that kind of thing. The output quality goes up, the cost goes up, but the semantics the developer sees are exactly the same as what they'd expect from any other provider.

And honestly, we think that's one of the underappreciated advantages of the diffusion approach. The compute-quality tradeoff is smooth and continuous. You don't have a binary "thinking on, thinking off." You have a dial, and the dial is doing something principled. Exposing it through a familiar interface was the obvious way to let people discover that without having to understand diffusion at all.

r001.rationale: The response says developers can use their existing OpenAI-shaped integrations and reasoning-effort knob, avoiding a new abstraction or integration rewrite to try Mercury.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to give developers a simple way to control the trade-off between latency and quality. With a diffusion language model, you generate through iterative refinement, so you have a natural knob: how much computation you spend refining the answer. You can use fewer steps when speed matters, or spend more compute when the task benefits from it.

Exposing that through an OpenAI-compatible reasoning-effort parameter makes it easy to use in existing applications. Developers don’t need to understand the details of the diffusion process or build a new integration. It’s a familiar interface, even though the mechanism underneath is different: here, the extra compute goes into additional refinement.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the familiar OpenAI-compatible parameter works in existing applications and requires no new integration, clearly explaining how it lowers the adoption barrier.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to give developers a simple way to control the trade-off between latency and output quality. With a diffusion language model, you can vary how much computation you spend refining the output at inference time. You can take fewer steps when speed matters, or spend more steps when the task benefits from additional refinement.

Exposing that through an OpenAI-compatible reasoning-effort parameter makes it easy to use within existing applications. You don’t have to understand the details of the diffusion sampler or build a separate integration to explore that trade-off. It’s a familiar interface for controlling the inference compute budget, even though the mechanism underneath is different.

r001.rationale: The response says the OpenAI-compatible parameter is easy to use in existing applications and avoids needing a separate integration, clearly conveying a lower adoption barrier.
